summary: SCTP puts a 32-bit checksum in each packet to check for damage. If another layer, such as DTLS, already gives the same or better protection, computing it wastes effort. This document provides a simple way for SCTP endpoints to agree to skip the checksum in that case.

plainLanguage.summary: Each package has a little sticker to prove it was not damaged. If the package is already sealed in a strong box that checks for damage, you can skip the sticker and save time.

questions: what is the zero checksum acceptable parameter
subtitle: How two SCTP endpoints can agree to skip the CRC32c checksum when another layer already protects the data.

tldr.problem: SCTP computes a 32-bit CRC32c checksum on every packet, which wastes processing when another method, such as DTLS, already provides the same or better data integrity.
tldr.mechanism: An endpoint announces a Zero Checksum Acceptable parameter in its INIT or INIT ACK chunk, naming an alternate error detection method, and its peer may then send packets whose checksum is zero.
tldr.outcome: Computing and verifying the checksum can be skipped in a backwards-compatible way, with SCTP over DTLS as the first defined alternate method.

today: RFC 9653 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2024, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the Zero Checksum Acceptable parameter and registers SCTP over DTLS as the first alternate error detection method.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SCTP (RFC 9260) uses a CRC32c checksum to provide some level of data integrity. When SCTP runs over DTLS (RFC 8261), the checksum adds no protection beyond what DTLS already gives, yet computing it at both the sender and the receiver still costs computing resources. That matters most for endpoints with limited computing power.

This document lets an SCTP endpoint declare, during association setup, that it accepts packets with a checksum of zero when a specific alternate error detection method is in use. Endpoints that support the extension stay interoperable with endpoints that do not. To keep this compatibility, endpoints using the extension must still implement CRC32c.
sections.plainLanguage: If a box is already locked in a safe that detects tampering, there is no need to also add a tamper sticker. This lets computers skip the extra sticker when both agree.

sections.title: Alternate Error Detection Methods
sections.content:
The CRC32c checksum covers the SCTP common header and the chunks in the packet. Unlike the TCP and UDP checksums, it does not use a pseudo header. Zero is a valid result of the algorithm, so a receiver that sees a checksum of zero cannot tell whether the sender skipped the computation or the computation really gave zero. If the receiver is willing to use an alternate error detection method, this ambiguity does not matter.

An alternate error detection method has two requirements:

  1. It MUST provide an equal or lower probability of false negatives than CRC32c. This MAY apply only to packets meeting some method-specific constraints.
  2. It MUST NOT cause a path failure lasting more than two retransmission timeouts (RTOs) because of middleboxes that expect correct CRC32c checksums.

The RFC gives DTLS as lower layer for SCTP as a method that meets both. SCTP Authentication (RFC 4895) meets the first, but only for packets whose first chunk is an AUTH chunk, and without a heuristic it does not meet the second.
sections.plainLanguage: You may only skip the sticker if the replacement check is at least as good, and if nobody along the road, like a checkpoint guard who insists on the sticker, would stop the package.

sections.title: The Zero Checksum Acceptable Parameter
sections.content:
The new chunk parameter has three fields: a 16-bit Type of 32769 (0x8001), a 16-bit Length that MUST be 8, and a 32-bit Error Detection Method Identifier (EDMID) that names the alternate method the sender is willing to use for packets it receives. Integers are in network byte order.

The parameter MAY appear in INIT and INIT ACK chunks, MUST NOT appear in any other chunk, and MUST NOT appear more than once in a chunk. An endpoint that does not support the extension skips it and processes the remaining parameters, because the two highest-order bits of the Type are 10, as RFC 9260 specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small note on the first message that says: I am happy to skip the sticker if we use this other kind of check. Computers that do not understand the note simply ignore it.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Procedures
sections.content:
An endpoint willing to accept zero checksums MUST include the parameter, naming its method, in the INIT or INIT ACK it sends. Its implementation MAY first require the upper layer to approve that method.

A sender may not use zero everywhere. It MUST use a correct CRC32c checksum if it has not received the parameter from its peer for a method it supports; in packets containing an INIT chunk; in responses to Out of the Blue (OOTB) packets; in packets containing a COOKIE ECHO chunk; in packets containing an ASCONF chunk when dynamic address reconfiguration (RFC 5061) is supported; and in packets that do not meet the method-specific constraints. The COOKIE ECHO and ASCONF rules keep implementations simpler, because finding the association for such packets can be more complex. If none of these restrictions apply, the sender SHOULD use zero.

A receiver that sent the parameter MUST accept both correct CRC32c packets and zero-checksum packets that meet the announced method's requirements. Otherwise it MUST drop all packets with an incorrect CRC32c checksum. It MAY also process OOTB packets with a zero checksum, which might speed up detecting association failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must say yes first. Even then, the very first hello and a few special messages still carry the real sticker. After that, the sticker can be skipped.

sections.title: Using DTLS and the Socket Option
sections.content:
SCTP over DTLS provides a stronger error detection method than CRC32c. Middleboxes cannot see the unencrypted SCTP packet, so there is no risk of interfering with a zero checksum, and DTLS encapsulation adds no method-specific constraints.

For socket programmers, the RFC describes a write-only SCTP_ACCEPT_ZERO_CHECKSUM option at the IPPROTO_SCTP level. It applies only to future associations. Its value is SCTP_EDMID_NONE, which disables alternate methods, or SCTP_EDMID_LOWER_LAYER_DTLS. The default is that alternate methods are disabled, and an implementation might only send zero checksums if the peer's announced method is also enabled locally. This section is informational only.
sections.plainLanguage: When the package is already inside a locked, tamper-proof box, nobody on the road can open it, so there is no reason to keep the sticker. An application also has a switch to say whether it allows this.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned chunk parameter type 32769 (0x8001) for Zero Checksum Acceptable. It also created a new "Error Detection Method" registry, with new entries handled under the Specification Required policy (RFC 8126).

A new method must be documented with its name and a specification that explains the method, why it has an equal or lower false-negative probability than CRC32c, any method-specific constraints, and why it does not cause path failures longer than two RTOs. Initially, value 0 is Reserved, value 1 is SCTP over DTLS, and values 2 to 4294967295 are unassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a public list of the approved replacement checks. Today it has one entry, DTLS, and anyone who wants to add another must prove it is just as good.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document does not change the security considerations in RFC 9260. Because of the first requirement, an alternate error detection method gives data integrity equal to or better than CRC32c. Because of the second, middleboxes that expect correct CRC32c checksums cannot cause permanent path failures.
sections.plainLanguage: Skipping the sticker is only allowed when the other check is at least as good, so packages are no less safe than before.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the parameter in bytes; MUST be 8.

fields.name: EDMID
fields.desc: Error Detection Method Identifier: the alternate method the sender is willing to use for received packets.
